stories.title: After Pentagon Official Took Office, His Family Firm’s Clients Won Up to $3.5 Billion in Military Contracts
stories.text: No paywalls. No advertisers. No billionaire owners. Just journalism that answers only to you. A senior War Department official who pledged to sell his stake in his family’s defense consulting firm still owns between $1 million and $5 million in the company over a year after his confirmation, according to his financial disclosures. The official, Michael Dodd, is the assistant secretary of war for critical technologies. His office writes the Pentagon’s technology roadmaps, which lay out what technologies the military needs as well as plans and funding strategies to develop them. In a September 2026 interview , he said these responsibilities give him “significant influence on what the services procure.” The firm he founded, Dioltas, helps companies move “critical technology” through the Pentagon contracting process, “from first relationship to strategic partnership to funding.” Dodd’s wife, Melanie, was the registered agent and treasurer for Dioltas until November, and their son Keegan is its manager, according to government filings. stories.author: The Lever team
stories.title: Jensen Huang’s Scandal Just Hit Your Pension
stories.text: When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned earlier this month amid revelations of his extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy, it didn’t just temporarily wipe out more than $1 trillion in the AI chipmaker’s value and disrupt the entire market — it also briefly deleted billions from public workers’ retirement plans. “The amount of losses that pension plans took just based off of his [resignation] was the equivalent of about a quarter of all of the money that was put into pension funds from state and local governments last year,” said Anthony Randazzo, founder and CEO of the bipartisan pension research and reform group Equable. While much of that loss was negated on Monday — when Nvidia notched its biggest single-day rally since 2003 after announcing it was reinstating Huang — the upheaval highlights how market concentration in the volatile artificial intelligence industry is leaving pensioners, state budgets, and taxpayers caught in the crossfire. Data published this month by Equable found that 24 of the largest public pension funds in the U.S. reported $59 billion in collective Nvidia holdings. stories.author: Judd Legum
stories.title: Amazon’s $5 deception
stories.text: Last week, Amazon users in New York City were met with a pop-up on the Amazon website and app stating that “ NYC Council could add up to $5 per order .” The claim was referring to legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act , that would require logistics companies like Amazon to change the way they employ delivery workers. Amazon relies on a network of over 40 contracted third-party delivery companies, or delivery service partners (DSPs), to complete its deliveries in New York City. Supporters of the Delivery Protection Act argue that Amazon’s use of a network of subcontractors allows both Amazon and the third-party companies to avoid responsibility for worker safety and protects Amazon from liability issues. Using subcontractors also allows Amazon to escape accountability, as it can just cancel a contract to avoid responsibility for a delivery worker’s conduct. The Delivery Protection Act would require companies like Amazon to directly employ delivery workers. stories.title: Don’t F#*k It Up, Democrats, Ep. 7: The Anti-Fascist Fight For Affordability
stories.text: Democrats made affordability the centerpiece of their midterm campaigns and won big. But what if the cost-of-living crisis isn't just an economic issue? What if it's a democracy issue? In Episode 7 of Don't F#*k It Up, Democrats (watch above or here ) , David Sirota speaks with Isabella Weber, an economist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and author of the new book Anti-Fascist Economics: In Defense of Affordability, Dignity, and Democracy . Weber explains how economic insecurity fuels authoritarianism, how the corporate-friendly economic policies Democrats have championed for decades may have helped pave the way for Trump, and why delivering on affordability will require taking on some of the world's most powerful corporations. They explore what Democrats should actually do to bring down the cost of living and restore people's faith in democracy. stories.title: Palestinians in Gaza Are Lining Their Tents with Sandbags to Stop Israeli Bullets
stories.text: Tareq Abu Adhra fortifies a side of his makeshift shelter with sandbags to protect from Israeli gunfire, in the Bir 19 encampment in Khan Younis. Story by Mohamed Ahmed and Sharif Abdel Kouddous KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip—Nofal Al-Akhras filled another empty flour sack with sand, tied off the top, and heaved it onto the other bags lining the outside of his tent in the Bir 19 area of the southern Gaza Strip. A displacement camp in a desolate sandy expanse west of Khan Younis, Bir 19 lies close to the yellow line where occupying Israeli troops are stationed. Al-Akhras stacked the sandbags three high, at about waist level, among drying laundry hung on a sagging clothesline, forming a makeshift barrier—a desperate attempt to protect himself and his family from Israeli gunfire. “Every day, around the clock, we are caught off guard by stray, deadly bullets fired indiscriminately,” he told Drop Site News. “We have lost many loved ones who were martyred by stray bullets striking displacement tents for no reason whatsoever.
